6.text: In other cases, more direct preliminary negotiations are entered into.

7.text: The father or the uncle of the bridegroom goes to the house of the bride to

8.text: ask permission for the suit. This preliminary asking is expressed by means

9.text: of various derivatives of the verb ñeweˊwg̣irkɪn (“thou askest for a wife”).

10.text: The suitor’s representative begins by going to the woods and bringing a large

11.text: bundle of fuel. This is one of the most unpleasant household duties. At the

12.text: same time, it is never done by guests, but either by poor men or by those

13.text: taking part in the cares of the household. Thus the young man’s representa-

14.text: tive shows by his act that he is a suitor, and that he wants to share in the

15.text: household duties. Then follows the first talk. The father of the bride

16.text: usually shows ill-will and displeasure. He tries to recall to mind every possible

17.text: reason for quarrelling and for a refusal of the suit, especially any awkward

18.text: acts. For instance, Meˊwet, a man from the Dry Anui, told me that before

19.text: he was married, his father-in-law had bitterly reproached his father, who acted

20.text: as suitor, because a few months before, while they were travelling together,

21.text: Meˊwet had driven faster than he had himself. Since the Chukchee are very

22.text: jealous concerning the speed of their reindeer,¹ it is considered rather forward,

23.text: on the part of a young man, to drive faster than those who are older. For

24.text: this reason young men, when they begin to think of some young girl, always

25.text: endeavor to be respectful to her father.

26.text: The “asking for a wife” lasts several days or even weeks. The suitor’s

27.text: representative works all the time, notwithstanding his age, gathers fuel, and

28.text: tends the herd, helping the herdsmen. At the same time he tries to gain the

29.text: good-will of his stubborn host. He praises the bridegroom and his whole

30.text: family, and does not desist, notwithstanding all the displeasure shown by his

31.text: host. At last the latter relents, and says, “Well, what can I do! Go home,

32.text: it is enough!” or something to the same effect. This is meant as an affirma-
